title: From Shipwreck to Runway: 300-Year-Old Wood Becomes High Fashion
summary:
Shipwrecks are usually studied for their history, not for their fashion potential. But a team of scientists and designers in Finland recently gave 300-year-old shipwreck wood a surprising new purpose: they turned it into two elegant, floor-length dresses.

The wood came from the "Hahtiperä wreck," a cargo vessel dating back to the 1600s. Its remains were found under a hotel parking lot in Oulu, Finland, during a 2019 renovation. Archeologists from the Finnish Heritage Agency preserved the ship's main hull, but some of the wet wood was too damaged to save. Instead of discarding it, the agency asked Aalto University to give the historic wood a second life.

Researchers there had previously created sustainable textile fibers from materials like paper and cardboard. They were eager to test the same eco-friendly process, called the "Ioncell method," on wood. First, they cut the wood into small pieces and shaved off the outer layers to remove centuries of dirt. The clean, inner wood was shredded into pulp and combined with a non-toxic salt-based solvent. The resulting mixture was spun into strong, smooth yarn.

Wood contains cellulose, the same natural material found in cotton and linen. Because of this, the new wood fiber was very strong. In fact, the scientists said it felt like silk and was stronger than cotton. To honor the shipwreck's history, the team did not use dye or bleach. Instead, the yarn kept its natural tan-brown color and slight shine from the old wood.

Textile designer Anna-Mari Leppisaari took on the challenge of turning the yarn into clothing. She created a unique pattern inspired by wood grain and computer pixels. The pattern was fed into an industrial knitting machine, which transformed the yarn into two identical, elegant dresses. Each dress was knitted as a single, seamless piece, creating no waste.

One dress is on display at the "Tomorrow's Wardrobe" exhibition at the Oulu Art Museum through September 2026. The second will be shown at Aalto University's "Designs for a Cooler Planet" exhibition from September to October 2026. Together, they show how old materials can be reused in new ways while sharing the story of the historic shipwreck. As researcher Pirjo Kääriäinen said, "If something this beautiful can be made from centuries-old wood, why do we keep throwing away materials that could still be circulated and reused?"
why_it_matters: This is a working example of the 'circular economy' — designing products so their materials get reused instead of dumped. Textile production is one of the world's most polluting industries, so turning even 300-year-old wreck timber into wearable fibre hints at a future where clothing does not depend on new cotton fields or oil-based plastics.

background_read: Aalto University (a Finnish university with campuses in Espoo and Helsinki) helped develop the Ioncell method together with researchers at the University of Helsinki. It uses ionic liquids — salt-like liquids — to dissolve cellulose without the harsh chemicals that older fibre-making processes depend on.

The best-known man-made fibre from wood is viscose, also called rayon, and it has been made since the late 1800s. Its classic production route uses carbon disulfide, a chemical that is harmful to workers and the environment, which is one reason greener methods such as Ioncell attract attention.

Waterlogged shipwrecks survive because mud and water keep oxygen out, so the wood does not rot. Once such timber dries, it can crumble, which is why archaeologists must keep it wet or treat it with special chemicals — one reason badly damaged pieces sometimes cannot be preserved.

Old wooden vessels were often recycled in a very literal way: after a ship was abandoned, its hull might be used as landfill or as the base for new buildings, which is how wrecks end up under streets and car parks.
Textiles are a major source of waste, with vast amounts of clothing burned or sent to landfill every year, so scientists are testing ways to turn old clothes, cardboard and even wood into new fibres.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — waste becomes value and story
perspectives.description: The project shows that material which would have been discarded can become something beautiful and useful, and the museum exhibitions give the public a way to see it. The dresses also carry the wreck's history, so a scientific experiment doubles as storytelling about a 1600s cargo ship.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — two dresses are not a system
perspectives.description: A sceptic would point out that this is a demonstration, not a production line: two dresses, made in a laboratory, using energy and specialist equipment most factories do not have. If the fibre stays expensive or difficult to scale, it will not reduce textile waste in any meaningful way.

Humans have made fibre from wood and reused cloth for a very long time — rag paper was made from worn-out clothing for centuries, and viscose fibre from wood dates back to the 1800s. Seen that way, the Ioncell method is less a brand-new invention than an old instinct about reuse upgraded with modern chemistry that avoids toxic solvents.

The next question is scale and economics: can such fibres be made cheaply enough, with clean enough energy, to compete with cotton and polyester? Museums can display pilot projects, but the real test is whether mills, brands and recycling systems adopt the technology before the exhibitions close.
